nodes.label: Abdülmecid I
nodes.full: Abdülmecid, 16 at his accession, ruled through the statesmen of the Tanzimat, issued the edicts of 1839 and 1856, moved the court from Topkapı to the new Dolmabahçe Palace in 1856, and led the empire through the Crimean War and the first foreign loans; his reign marked the shift of power from the palace to the Sublime Porte.
nodes.src: Roderic Davison, Reform in the Ottoman Empire 1856–1876 (1963); Stanford Shaw and Ezel Shaw, History of the Ottoman Empire and Modern Turkey vol. 2 (1977).

nodes.label: Reşid, Âli and Fuad Pasha
nodes.full: Mustafa Reşid Pasha, who had been ambassador in Paris and London and drafted the Gülhane edict, and his pupils Mehmed Emin Âli Pasha and Fuad Pasha, who held the grand vizierate and the foreign ministry in turn for most of the years between 1846 and 1871, were the architects of the Tanzimat reforms, of the Reform Edict of 1856 and of the diplomacy of the Crimean War and after.
nodes.src: Davison 1963; Butrus Abu-Manneh, ‘The Islamic Roots of the Gülhane Rescript’, Die Welt des Islams 34 (1994).

nodes.label: Abdülaziz
nodes.full: Abdülaziz, the first sultan to visit western Europe, in 1867, built new palaces and an ironclad fleet, the third largest in the world in the 1870s, and presided over the growing debt and the default of 1875; he turned away from the reformers and was deposed by a coup of Midhat Pasha, Hüseyin Avni Pasha and the softas on 30 May 1876, and died a few days later in what was officially a suicide.
nodes.src: Davison 1963; Shaw and Shaw 1977; Carter Findley, Bureaucratic Reform in the Ottoman Empire (1980).

nodes.label: Midhat Pasha
nodes.full: Midhat Pasha, governor of the Danube province, which he reorganised in 1864–1868 with roads, schools and an agricultural bank, and later of Baghdad, was the leader of the constitutional movement and, as grand vizier in December 1876, the author of the constitution; Abdülhamid exiled him in February 1877, and he died in 1884 in prison at Taif, probably strangled.
nodes.src: Ali Haydar Midhat, The Life of Midhat Pasha (1903); Davison 1963; Shaw and Shaw 1977.

nodes.label: Abdülhamid II
nodes.full: Abdülhamid II, who came to the throne on 31 August 1876 after the brief reign and breakdown of Murad V, promised a constitution, opened the parliament in 1877 and suspended it in February 1878; for thirty years he ruled from the Yıldız palace through personal control, a large network of informers, censorship, and a policy of pan-Islam, of building schools, railways and telegraphs and of managing the great powers.
nodes.src: Selim Deringil, The Well-Protected Domains (1998); Şükrü Hanioğlu, A Brief History of the Late Ottoman Empire (2008); François Georgeon, Abdülhamid II (2003).

nodes.label: Murad V
nodes.full: Murad V, a prince of liberal sympathies who had met Namık Kemal and the Young Ottomans, reigned for 93 days before the physicians declared him mentally ill after a breakdown; he spent the remaining 28 years of his life in the Çırağan palace, and a failed attempt to restore him in 1878, led by Ali Suavi, who was killed, is a famous episode.
nodes.src: Davison 1963; Georgeon 2003; Shaw and Shaw 1977.

nodes.label: Crimean War
nodes.full: A dispute with Russia over the Holy Places and the czar's claim to protect Orthodox subjects led to war in October 1853; the Russian fleet destroyed an Ottoman squadron at Sinope on 30 November, and Britain and France joined in March 1854, with Piedmont in 1855; after the long siege of Sevastopol the Treaty of Paris of 30 March 1856 neutralised the Black Sea and admitted the empire to the Concert of Europe. Ottoman losses were heavy, with deaths, mostly from disease, put at about 100,000.
nodes.src: Treaty of Paris (1856); Orlando Figes, Crimea (2010); Candan Badem, The Ottoman Crimean War (2010).

nodes.label: Mount Lebanon and Damascus
nodes.full: Violence between Druze and Maronites in Mount Lebanon from May 1860 spread to Zahle, Deir al-Qamar and Damascus, where Muslim crowds killed several thousand Christians in July; the death toll in the whole is put at between 5,000 and over 10,000. A French expedition landed in August, Fuad Pasha was sent with full powers and executed Ottoman officials, and the Règlement of 1861 gave Mount Lebanon a Christian governor.
nodes.src: Leila Fawaz, An Occasion for War (1994); Ussama Makdisi, The Culture of Sectarianism (2000); Règlement organique (1861).

nodes.label: Circassian expulsion
nodes.full: After the Russian conquest of the western Caucasus in 1864 several hundred thousand Circassians, Abkhaz and other Muslim peoples left or were expelled to the Ottoman Empire through the Black Sea ports, and thousands died of disease and cold; Circassians describe it as genocide, and Russia's historians usually as a migration and war loss, while the Ottomans settled most in the Balkans and Anatolia.
nodes.src: Kemal Karpat, Ottoman Population 1830–1914 (1985); Stephen Shenfield, ‘The Circassians: A Forgotten Genocide?’, in The Massacre in History (1999); Justin McCarthy, Death and Exile (1995).

nodes.label: Bulgarian uprising
nodes.full: A poorly prepared rising in the Bulgarian lands, one of a series of revolts after Herzegovina in 1875, was put down by irregular bashibazouks and troops with massacres in Batak and other villages in which some 15,000 were killed in estimates running up to 30,000 or more; reports by the American journalist MacGahan and Gladstone's pamphlet on the Bulgarian Horrors turned European opinion against the Porte.
nodes.src: Richard Millman, Britain and the Eastern Question 1875–1878 (1979); Gladstone, Bulgarian Horrors (1876); Mark Mazower, The Balkans (2000).

nodes.label: Russo-Turkish war
nodes.full: Russia declared war in April 1877 after the conference at Constantinople failed; Osman Pasha's defence of Plevna delayed the Russians until 10 December, and after the crossing of the Balkans and the fall of Adrianople an armistice was signed in January 1878; the armistice and the Treaty of San Stefano of 3 March, which created a large Bulgaria, led to a crisis with Britain and Austria.
nodes.src: William Allen and Paul Muratoff, Caucasian Battlefields (1953); Treaty of San Stefano (1878); Shaw and Shaw 1977.

nodes.label: Hamidian massacres
nodes.full: Following the suppression of an Armenian revolt in Sasun in 1894 and the powers' reform proposals of 1895, massacres of Armenians took place in Trebizond, Erzurum, Diyarbakır, Sivas, Urfa and many other places in 1895–1896, and in Istanbul after the Armenian Revolutionary Federation seized the Ottoman Bank on 26 August 1896; contemporary estimates run from 80,000 to 300,000 dead, and the events are part of the background to 1915.
nodes.src: Vahakn Dadrian, The History of the Armenian Genocide (1995); Selim Deringil, ‘The Armenian Question Is Finally Closed’, Comparative Studies in Society and History 51 (2009); Hanioğlu 2008.

nodes.label: Cretan revolt and Greek war
nodes.full: Cretan Christians rose in 1866–1869, with the siege of the monastery of Arkadi where hundreds were killed, and again in 1896; Greek forces intervened and in the war of April–May 1897 the Ottoman army under Edhem Pasha, trained by German officers, beat the Greeks in Thessaly in thirty days, though the powers made the sultan accept the autonomy of Crete under Prince George of Greece.
nodes.src: Davison 1963; Douglas Dakin, The Unification of Greece (1972); Treaty of Constantinople (1897).

nodes.label: Congress of Berlin
nodes.full: The Congress under Bismarck revised San Stefano: Bulgaria was reduced and made an autonomous principality with Eastern Rumelia a separate province, Serbia, Montenegro and Romania were recognised as independent, Bosnia and Herzegovina went to Austrian administration, Kars, Ardahan and Batum to Russia, and Cyprus was to be occupied by Britain by a separate convention of 4 June; the Ottomans lost a large part of their European territory and population.
nodes.src: Treaty of Berlin (13 July 1878); Cyprus Convention (4 June 1878); William Langer, European Alliances and Alignments (1931).

nodes.label: Gülhane edict
nodes.full: The Imperial Edict of the Rose Chamber, read by Mustafa Reşid Pasha before the sultan, the ministers, the ulema and the foreign diplomats in the Gülhane park, promised security of life, honour and property to all subjects regardless of religion, an end to tax farming, regular conscription and fair trial; it opened the period of the Tanzimat, the reorganisation.
nodes.src: Hatt-ı Şerif of Gülhane (1839); Davison 1963; Abu-Manneh 1994.

nodes.label: Reform Edict
nodes.full: The Islahat Fermanı, issued during the peace conference at Paris and drafted under pressure from Britain and France, promised equality of all subjects regardless of religion, access to schools and offices, the end of the distinction in taxes and military service, and the freedom to build churches and schools; the principle of equality, which Muslim conservatives opposed, was a central issue of the next decades.
nodes.src: Hatt-ı Hümayun (1856); Davison 1963; Findley 1980.

nodes.label: Land Code and vilayet law
nodes.full: The Land Code of 1858 recognised hereditary use of state land by registered holders and stimulated registration, which in places let notables register communal land; the Provincial Law of 1864, based on the French departmental model, divided the empire into vilayets, sancaks and kazas with appointed governors and elected councils, and became the basis of local government until 1913.
nodes.src: Land Code (1858); Vilayet Law (1864); Huri İslamoğlu-İnan (ed.), The Ottoman Empire and the World-Economy (1987).

nodes.label: Mecelle and Council of State
nodes.full: A commission led by Ahmed Cevdet Pasha compiled, between 1869 and 1876, the Mecelle, a civil code in 1,851 articles taken from Hanafi jurisprudence, the first codification of Islamic law in a modern form; with the Council of State, the new nizamiye courts and the commercial code of 1850, it began a dual legal system of sharia and secular courts.
nodes.src: Mecelle-i Ahkâm-ı Adliyye (1876); Findley 1980; Niyazi Berkes, The Development of Secularism in Turkey (1964).

nodes.label: Constitution of 1876
nodes.full: The Kanun-ı Esasi, drafted by a commission under Midhat Pasha, was proclaimed on the day the powers' conference met at Constantinople; it provided for a bicameral parliament, with an elected chamber and an appointed senate, the equality of all Ottomans, and left the sultan with the power to exile persons deemed dangerous to the state, which Abdülhamid used against Midhat. The parliament met in March 1877 and was dissolved in February 1878; the constitution was not abolished but suspended until 1908.
nodes.src: Kanun-ı Esasi (1876); Robert Devereux, The First Ottoman Constitutional Period (1963); Davison 1963.

nodes.label: Public Debt Administration
nodes.full: After the default of 1875 and the war, the Decree of Muharrem set up in December 1881 an international body, with representatives of the bondholders of Britain, France, Germany, Austria, Italy and the Ottoman Bank, which took over the revenue from salt, tobacco, stamps, silk and spirits and the fisheries to service the debt; it employed several thousand officials and controlled a large share of the state's income.
nodes.src: Decree of Muharrem (1881); Donald Blaisdell, European Financial Control in the Ottoman Empire (1929); Şevket Pamuk, The Ottoman Empire and European Capitalism (1987).

nodes.label: Education law and schools
nodes.full: The Public Education Regulation of 1869 set up primary and secondary schools, teacher training and a university, and under Abdülhamid II the number of state schools grew rapidly, with thousands of primary schools, some 600 middle schools (rüşdiye) by 1908, and military and professional academies, among them the Imperial School of Law (1878) and Medicine; the schools produced the officers and officials of the 1908 revolution.
nodes.src: Maarif-i Umumiye Nizamnamesi (1869); Benjamin Fortna, Imperial Classroom (2002); Selçuk Akşin Somel, The Modernization of Public Education in the Ottoman Empire (2001).

nodes.label: Bulgarian Exarchate
nodes.full: A firman of 1870 created an autonomous Bulgarian church, the Exarchate, under an exarch in Istanbul, independent of the Greek patriarchate, with jurisdiction over dioceses where two thirds of the Orthodox population voted for it; the Patriarchate declared it schismatic in 1872, and the church became both a religious body and the basis for the Bulgarian national movement.
nodes.src: Firman of 28 February 1870; Mazower 2000; Richard Crampton, A Concise History of Bulgaria (1997).

nodes.label: Armenian constitution
nodes.full: After a decade of struggles between the amiras and the artisans and professionals, the Armenian Patriarchate in 1863 was given a constitution with a national assembly of 140 members, elected, with two thirds of laymen, and a civil and a religious council; it was the best-known of the millet constitutions, which Greeks and Jews followed in smaller forms.
nodes.src: Hagop Barsoumian, The Armenian Amira Class of Istanbul (2007); Richard Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People vol. 2 (1997).

nodes.label: Pan-Islam
nodes.full: Abdülhamid II emphasised his role as caliph of all Muslims after the loss of the Balkan provinces and the French and British expansion in Muslim lands, sent emissaries to Central Asia, Africa and India, built the Hejaz Railway as a work of the Muslim world, and gave the Ottoman state a stress on Islamic symbols; the policy helped to rally subjects, though it did little in foreign politics.
nodes.src: Deringil 1998; Jacob Landau, The Politics of Pan-Islam (1990); Hanioğlu 2008.

nodes.label: Baha’u’llah
nodes.full: Baha'u'llah, the founder of the Baha'i faith, was banished from Baghdad to Istanbul and Edirne in 1863–1868, where in 1866 he declared his mission publicly to Babis, and then to the prison city of Acre in 1868, where he lived until his death in 1892; the Baha'i World Centre at Haifa and Acre derives from this exile.
nodes.src: Moojan Momen, The Bábí and Baháʼí Religions (1981); Juan Cole, Modernity and the Millennium (1998).

nodes.label: Robert College
nodes.full: American Protestant missionaries began in the 1820s, built schools at Bebek (Robert College, 1863), the Syrian Protestant College at Beirut (1866) and Anatolian colleges, and educated generations of Armenians, Bulgarians, Greeks and Arabs; the missions, though they won few converts from Orthodoxy and Islam, produced a large part of the new intelligentsia and drew the suspicion of the government.
nodes.src: Frank Andrews Stone, Academies for Anatolia (1984); Ussama Makdisi, Artillery of Heaven (2008).

nodes.label: Dolmabahçe and Yıldız
nodes.full: Dolmabahçe Palace on the Bosphorus, built by the Armenian architects Karabet and Nikoğos Balyan between 1843 and 1856 in an eclectic style of Baroque, neoclassical and Ottoman elements, with 285 rooms, replaced the Topkapı as the imperial residence; Abdülhamid II preferred the smaller, defensible Yıldız complex on the hill above, with its pavilions and a theatre.
nodes.src: Doğan Kuban, Ottoman Architecture (2010); Ahmet Ersoy, Architecture and the Late Ottoman Historical Imaginary (2015).

nodes.label: Tanzimat press and novel
nodes.full: Şinasi and Agah Efendi started Tercüman-ı Ahval, the first private Turkish newspaper, in 1860, and Şinasi's Tasvir-i Efkâr in 1862; the Tanzimat novel began with Şemsettin Sami's Taaşşuk-ı Talat ve Fitnat (1872) and Namık Kemal's İntibah (1876), then Ahmed Midhat and Recaizade Mahmud Ekrem; the press and the novel gave a new public sphere and language.
nodes.src: Berkes 1964; Şerif Mardin, The Genesis of Young Ottoman Thought (1962); Hanioğlu 2008.

nodes.label: Namık Kemal’s play
nodes.full: Namık Kemal's patriotic play on the defence of Silistra in 1854, staged at the Gedikpaşa theatre in April 1873, produced demonstrations of enthusiasm and its author's exile to Cyprus by the government, which saw its calls for the homeland (vatan) and liberty as subversive; it is regarded as a founding moment of Turkish nationalist feeling.
nodes.src: Namık Kemal, Vatan yahut Silistre (1873); Mardin 1962; Berkes 1964.

nodes.label: Osman Hamdi
nodes.full: Osman Hamdi, a painter trained in Paris with Gérôme and the first Ottoman archaeologist of repute, directed the Imperial Museum from 1881, discovered the royal necropolis of Sidon with the Alexander Sarcophagus (1887), secured the law of 1884 on antiquities that kept finds in the empire, built the Archaeological Museum (1891) and painted The Tortoise Trainer (1906).
nodes.src: Edhem Eldem, Osman Hamdi Bey (2010); Wendy Shaw, Possessing Ottoman Antiquities (2003).

nodes.label: Hamidian photography
nodes.full: Photographers such as the Armenian Abdullah Frères, court photographers from 1863, and the Sébah and Joaillier studios produced portraits and views of the empire, and in 1893 Abdülhamid II had albums of some 1,800 photographs of the provinces, schools and works made and sent to the Library of Congress and the British Museum as a record of the state's progress.
nodes.src: Engin Çizgen, Photography in the Ottoman Empire (1987); Carney Gavin, Imperial Self-Portrait (1988).

nodes.label: Ottomanism
nodes.full: The Tanzimat statesmen's idea of a common Ottoman citizenship of all subjects regardless of religion, defined in the Edicts of 1839 and 1856 and the nationality law of 1869, was meant to counter separatism and European intervention, but Muslims saw it as a loss of privilege and Christians as insufficient, and its failure was the background of the nationalisms of the late empire.
nodes.src: Nationality Law (1869); Davison 1963; Kemal Karpat, The Politicization of Islam (2001).

nodes.label: Young Ottomans
nodes.full: A group of writers and officials, Namık Kemal, Ziya Pasha, Ali Suavi and Ağah Efendi among them, founded a secret society in 1865, fled to Paris and London in 1867 and published newspapers that called for a constitution and an elected assembly based on the Islamic principle of consultation; Prince Mustafa Fazıl Pasha of Egypt financed them, and their ideas took form in the constitution of 1876.
nodes.src: Şerif Mardin, The Genesis of Young Ottoman Thought (1962); Hanioğlu 2008.

nodes.label: al-Afghani
nodes.full: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, the Persian-born agitator, lectured in Istanbul in 1870 and was expelled after a speech on the prophets and philosophers, then returned in 1892 at Abdülhamid's invitation and lived under watch until his death in 1897; his call for pan-Islamic unity and reform and his pupil Muhammad Abduh's modernism shaped Muslim thought in the empire and beyond.
nodes.src: Nikki Keddie, Sayyid Jamāl ad-Dīn ‘al-Afghānī’ (1972); Albert Hourani, Arabic Thought in the Liberal Age (1962).

nodes.label: Committee of Union and Progress
nodes.full: Medical students at the military medical school in Istanbul founded in 1889 a secret society, İttihad-ı Osmanî, which later took the name Committee of Union and Progress; its exiled members in Paris and Geneva, among them Ahmed Rıza, a positivist, and Prince Sabahaddin, a liberal, published Meşveret and Şûrâ-yı Ümmet and organised the congresses of the Ottoman opposition in 1902 and 1907.
nodes.src: Şükrü Hanioğlu, The Young Turks in Opposition (1995); Hanioğlu 2008.

nodes.label: Turkist writing
nodes.full: The Hungarian orientalist Arminius Vámbéry and the Turkish writers Ahmed Vefik Pasha, Şemsettin Sami and Ahmed Midhat began to treat the Turks as a historic people with a language and a past, and in 1904 the Tatar Yusuf Akçura, writing in Cairo, set out in Üç Tarz-ı Siyaset the choice between Ottomanism, pan-Islam and Turkish nationalism and argued for the last.
nodes.src: Yusuf Akçura, Üç Tarz-ı Siyaset (1904); David Kushner, The Rise of Turkish Nationalism (1977).

nodes.label: Loans and default
nodes.full: The first foreign loan was taken in 1854 to pay for the Crimean War, and fifteen more followed, so that the nominal debt rose to some 200 million pounds by 1875 with a large part of it to cover the old deficits; in October 1875 the government declared that it would pay half the interest in bonds and in 1876 stopped payment, and bondholders' agitation led to the Debt Administration.
nodes.src: Blaisdell 1929; Pamuk 1987; Donald Quataert, The Ottoman Empire 1700–1922 (2000).

nodes.label: Ottoman Bank and Régie
nodes.full: The Imperial Ottoman Bank, a British and French institution founded in 1863 as the state's bank, issued the banknotes, acted as the treasury's agent and financed the debt; in 1883 the Tobacco Régie, a company of European bondholders and the Ottoman Bank with a monopoly of the production and sale of tobacco, was given the revenue and a staff of thousands, a symbol of foreign control and a cause of strikes.
nodes.src: Edhem Eldem, A History of the Ottoman Bank (1999); Donald Quataert, Social Disintegration and Popular Resistance in the Ottoman Empire (1983).

nodes.label: Cash crops
nodes.full: The American Civil War raised the price of cotton and led to the extension of cotton in Çukurova, Izmir and Egypt in the 1860s, and the export of raisins, figs, tobacco and silk grew; by the early twentieth century the Ottoman export economy depended on agricultural goods sold to Britain, France, Germany and Austria in return for manufactured goods, with a persistent trade deficit.
nodes.src: Quataert 2000; Pamuk 1987; Reşat Kasaba, The Ottoman Empire and the World Economy (1988).

nodes.label: Railways
nodes.full: The first railway, Izmir–Aydın, opened in 1866 under a British concession, followed by the lines from Istanbul to Edirne and Vienna, and the German-financed Anatolian Railway reached Ankara in 1892 and Konya in 1896; the concession for the Baghdad Railway, signed in 1903, linked Konya to Baghdad and the Gulf and the empire to German politics.
nodes.src: Murat Özyüksel, The Berlin–Baghdad Railway and the Ottoman Empire (2014); Quataert 2000.

nodes.label: Telegraph
nodes.full: The first telegraph line, from Istanbul to Edirne and Shumen in 1855, to serve the army in the Crimean War, was extended to all provincial capitals by 1870 and the sultan, with a telegraph at the Yıldız palace, controlled information and the provincial administration; the system, along with the postal service of 1840, made centralisation possible.
nodes.src: Yakup Bektaş, ‘The Sultan's Messenger’, Technology and Culture 41 (2000); Quataert 2000.

nodes.label: Hejaz Railway
nodes.full: Abdülhamid II announced in 1900 a railway from Damascus to Mecca, to be built by Muslim donations and Ottoman labour under the German engineer Meissner Pasha; the line reached Medina on 1 September 1908 and shortened the pilgrimage from 40 days to 5, with a symbolic and a military value, though its extension to Mecca was never built.
nodes.src: William Ochsenwald, The Hijaz Railroad (1980); James Nicholson, The Hejaz Railway (2005).

nodes.label: Galata Bridge and Tünel
nodes.full: The first Galata Bridge, a wooden floating bridge, was opened in 1845 and the Tünel, a 573-metre funicular tunnel from Galata to Pera built by a French engineer, in 1875, the second oldest underground railway in the world; gas lighting, horse trams from 1871 and the first municipal organisation of the city, the Şehremaneti of 1855, transformed the capital's life.
nodes.src: Zeynep Çelik, The Remaking of Istanbul (1986); Stéphane Yérasimos, ‘Istanbul’.

nodes.label: Treaty of Paris
nodes.full: The treaty admitted the Ottoman Empire to the public law and concert of Europe, guaranteed its independence and integrity, neutralised the Black Sea and ended Russia's protectorate over the principalities and its claim to speak for the Orthodox; the powers' guarantee did not prevent their later interventions, but the Ottomans from 1856 were counted among the European states.
nodes.src: Treaty of Paris (1856); Anderson 1966; Davison 1963.

nodes.label: Cyprus and Egypt
nodes.full: By the Cyprus Convention of 4 June 1878 Britain took over the administration of the island in return for a promise to defend the Asian provinces; in 1882, after the Urabi revolt and the bombardment of Alexandria, a British army occupied Egypt at Tel el-Kebir on 13 September, and though the Ottoman sovereignty was formally unchanged, the two provinces were lost in practice.
nodes.src: Cyprus Convention (1878); Juan Cole, Colonialism and Revolution in the Middle East (1993); Anderson 1966.

nodes.label: German friendship
nodes.full: After the Berlin Congress Abdülhamid looked to Germany as a power without territorial claims, with a military mission under Colmar von der Goltz from 1883, the Anatolian and Baghdad railways and the state visits of Kaiser Wilhelm II in 1889 and in 1898, when he visited Jerusalem and Damascus and declared himself the friend of the 300 million Muslims.
nodes.src: Jonathan McMurray, Distant Ties: Germany, the Ottoman Empire, and the Construction of the Baghdad Railway (2001); Hanioğlu 2008.

nodes.label: Capitulations
nodes.full: The consular courts, the exemption from internal taxes, the low customs duties and the protection of Ottoman Christians by foreign embassies (berat holders) were extended by the Treaties of 1838–1841 and were seen by the Porte as the chief limit of its sovereignty; attempts to abolish them in 1856, 1869 and 1908 failed, and they were ended only in the First World War and Lausanne.
nodes.src: Maurits van den Boogert, The Capitulations and the Ottoman Legal System (2005); Davison 1963.

nodes.label: Muhacir movements
nodes.full: Some five to seven million Muslims from Crimea, the Caucasus, Bulgaria, Serbia, Bosnia and Thessaly came as refugees (muhacir) to Ottoman lands between 1856 and 1914, with peaks after the Crimean War, 1864 and 1877–1878; the state settled them in Anatolia and Syria through a Refugee Commission, with large numbers of deaths from hunger and typhus, and they changed the demography and the politics of the empire.
nodes.src: Kemal Karpat 1985; Justin McCarthy, Death and Exile (1995); Isa Blumi, Reinstating the Ottomans (2011).

nodes.label: Famine
nodes.full: Drought and harsh winters destroyed the harvests and flocks of central and eastern Anatolia, with tens of thousands of deaths, in estimates up to 250,000, and with a large flight to the towns; the famine coincided with the default and the Balkan crisis and the government's relief was limited by its finances.
nodes.src: Kemal Karpat 1985; Donald Quataert, The Ottoman Empire 1700–1922 (2000).

nodes.label: Census
nodes.full: The census of 1881–1882/1893 counted some 17.4 million subjects in the empire, of whom about three quarters were Muslims, with Christians in the Balkans and Anatolia forming a large part of the rest; Karpat's reconstruction shows an overall population of some 25 million in 1900 with a rise in the Muslim share by the loss of the Christian provinces and by refugee migrations.
nodes.src: Kemal Karpat, Ottoman Population 1830–1914 (1985); Justin McCarthy, The Population of the Ottoman Empire (1983).

nodes.label: Earthquake of 1894
nodes.full: A strong earthquake of 10 July 1894 in the Marmara, with magnitude of about 7.0, damaged the Grand Bazaar, mosques and houses in Istanbul and killed 474 people officially, with some thousand injured; the sultan ordered the rebuilding, with the architect Vallaury, whose neoclassical designs for the Grand Bazaar's repairs and the Archaeological Museum remade the look of the city.
nodes.src: Nicholas Ambraseys, Earthquakes in the Mediterranean and Middle East (2009); Çelik 1986.

nodes.label: Women’s journals
nodes.full: The first Ottoman women's periodical, Terakki-i Muhadderat (1869), was followed by Şükufezar (1886) and Hanımlara Mahsus Gazete (1895–1908), which published women authors, among them Fatma Aliye (1862–1936), the first Ottoman woman novelist, who in Muhazarat (1892) and with Ahmed Midhat's help wrote on women's rights, and the debates over veiling, polygamy and education began.
nodes.src: Serpil Çakır, Osmanlı Kadın Hareketi (1994); Elizabeth Frierson, ‘Unimagined Communities’, Critical Matrix 9 (1995); Deniz Kandiyoti.

nodes.label: Slave trade ended
nodes.full: The Ottoman government closed the Istanbul slave market in 1847 under British pressure, banned the trade from the Black Sea in 1857 and in the 1880s signed conventions with Britain; but the slave trade in Africans, which was part of household life in the Hijaz and Anatolia, and the Circassian girls in the harems of the upper class continued until the end of the century.
nodes.src: Ehud Toledano, The Ottoman Slave Trade and Its Suppression (1982); Madeline Zilfi, Women and Slavery in the Late Ottoman Empire (2010).

nodes.label: Circassian villages
nodes.full: The Circassians were settled in groups on the frontier of the Balkans and Anatolia and near Amman, Jerash and the Golan, in new villages with their own language and customs, and became an important element in the sultan's irregular cavalry and gendarmerie; the settlements also caused conflict with local Bedouins, Kurds and Christians over land and security.
nodes.src: Eugene Rogan, Frontiers of the State in the Late Ottoman Empire (1999); Karpat 1985.

nodes.label: Spies and censorship
nodes.full: Abdülhamid II's reign was marked by a pervasive system of surveillance by spies (jurnalcis) who reported on officials, writers and foreigners, an expanding censorship that banned words such as revolution and Armenia, and the exile of dissidents to Fezzan, Yemen and the Hejaz; at the same time there were more schools and newspapers than before.
nodes.src: Georgeon 2003; Hanioğlu 2008; Deringil 1998.

nodes.label: The Egyptian crisis and the last years of Mahmud II
nodes.full: The defeat at Nizip in June 1839 and Mahmud II’s death a week later left a boy sultan, the Egyptian fleet in Alexandria and the Tanzimat’s authors to rebuild the state with the guarantee of the powers.
nodes.src: background — see the Ottoman Empire 1683–1839 folio (ottoman-empire-1683-1839)
